etymology: From the Old English upbregdan, “to bring up against, to cast up” (up + bregdan, “to braid, to weave, to throw”); hence to throw a fault in a man’s face, to reproach him with what he has done or with what has been given him.
biblical_def: To upbraid is to cast a thing up in a man’s face — to reproach him, to twit him with his fault or with the favour he has received. The Authorized Version uses it in two directions, and both must be held. First, it is a right thing when the Lord Himself does it against impenitence: “Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not” (Mat 11:20). Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum had seen the mighty works and would not turn, and the Christ who wept over Jerusalem also charged them home. So too He “upbraided them with their unbelief and hardness of heart” (Mar 16:14) — and the men so upbraided were His own apostles. The Lord’s upbraiding is never spite; it is the surgeon’s knife, laid on that the patient may live. Second, and sweeter, is the great negative: God “giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not” (Jas 1:5). The beggar who comes to God for wisdom is not met with a recital of how often he has come before, nor with a reminder of how ill he used the last gift. There is no grudging in the Giver, no throwing of past mercies in the face of a present asker. Men give and then remind; God gives and forgets the reckoning. Sinful upbraiding is the other thing altogether — the men of Succoth “did upbraid” Gideon (Jdg 8:15), taunting a servant of the LORD in his weakness.
webster_summary: To charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach; to cast a fault or a favour in a man’s face.
webster_full: UPBRAID, to charge with something wrong or disgraceful; to reproach; to chide.
Also, to reproach a man with a benefit conferred — to cast the gift in his teeth.
From Old English upbregdan, “to bring up against,” to throw in the face.
Christ upbraided the cities that saw His works and repented not (Mat 11:20).
God giveth liberally and upbraideth not (Jas 1:5) — grace without grudging.
scriptures: Jas 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not:
Afterward he appeared unto the eleven as they sat at meat, and upbraided them with their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they believed not them which had seen him after he was risen.
Jdg 8:15

And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men that are weary?
corruption_summary: An age that cannot bear correction has abolished the Lord’s upbraiding, and an age that gives grudgingly has forgotten the God who upbraideth not.
corruption_paragraphs: The word is corrupted from two sides at once. On one side stands the pulpit that will not upbraid at all: Christ is preached as incapable of rebuke, His woes over Chorazin and Bethsaida quietly dropped, and every sharp word of the risen Lord to His own disciples explained away as a cultural artefact. That is not tenderness but cowardice, and it leaves the impenitent comfortable in their impenitence. Christ upbraided cities because He meant to save men out of them, and a ministry that has lost the note of charge has lost the note of rescue too. On the other side stands the professing Christian who upbraids constantly — the giver who never lets a gift be forgotten, the brother who keeps the ledger of every failure and reads it aloud whenever advantage requires. That man has learned neither from the Lord’s rebuke, which is surgical and aims at repentance, nor from the Lord’s giving, which keeps no ledger at all.

The principle to recover is the doubleness of Jas 1:5 held together with Mat 11:20 by one God who is not divided against Himself. He upbraids the unrepentant because He is holy, and He upbraideth not the asker because He is gracious; and the same mouth speaks both. This is unspeakable comfort for the weak believer who is ashamed to come again. He fears God will meet him with a reckoning — how many times already, how poorly used, how little improved. Scripture forecloses the fear: the Giver gives liberally, and upbraideth not. There is no sigh in heaven when a beggar comes back. Only let him come asking in faith, nothing wavering, for the reproach he dreads was borne away by the Son who was Himself reproached in his room and stead.
roots_summary: The word means to cast a fault, or a favour, in a man’s face — to reproach.
roots_lines: Upbraid — Old English upbregdan, “to bring up against, to throw in the face.”
It reproaches a man either with his sin or with the gift he was given.
Christ upbraided cities that saw the mighty works and repented not (Mat 11:20).
He upbraided His own apostles for unbelief and hardness of heart (Mar 16:14).
God gives liberally and upbraideth not — grace without a ledger (Jas 1:5).
usage: The Lord upbraids the impenitent city because He is holy, and upbraids His own because He loves them.
God upbraideth not: the beggar who comes back a hundredth time is met with a gift, not a reckoning.
To upbraid a man with the help you gave him is to give as the world gives, not as God gives.

etymology: From the Latin importunus, “troublesome, unfit, out of season” (in-, “not,” + portus, “a harbour” — that which affords no landing-place); hence to press a request without ceasing, to urge and urge again until the thing is granted.
biblical_def: To importune is to press a petition without leaving off — to ask, and ask again, and refuse to be dismissed. The Authorized Version carries the noun in the Lord’s own parable of the friend at midnight: “yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth” (Luk 11:8). The neighbour will not stir for friendship’s sake; he will stir because the knocking will not stop. So also the widow of Luk 18, who wearied an unjust judge by “her continual coming” (Luk 18:5) until he avenged her. Both parables are arguments from the lesser to the greater, and both are given for the same declared end: “that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1). The point is emphatically not that God is a grudging neighbour or an unjust judge who must be worn down. It is the opposite: if reluctance yields to persistence, how much more shall the Father who delights to give? “And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?” (Luk 18:7). Importunity is therefore not a lever upon God but a mark upon His elect — they are the ones who cry day and night. It is Jacob at Peniel refusing to loose his hold, and the Syrophenician woman answering the Lord’s own hard word with faith. The persevering asker is not manufacturing the answer; he is being conformed to a Giver who has already resolved to give.
webster_summary: To press or urge a request with troublesome frequency; to solicit without ceasing until the thing is obtained.
webster_full: IMPORTUNE, to request with urgency; to press with solicitation; to urge with frequent application.
IMPORTUNITY, pressing solicitation; urgent request; incessant or frequent application.
From Latin importunus, “troublesome, affording no harbour” — a suit that will not be put off.
The friend at midnight receives because of his importunity (Luk 11:8).
The widow’s continual coming wearied the unjust judge (Luk 18:5).
scriptures: Luk 11:8
I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.
Luk 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
Luk 18:5
Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.
Luk 18:7
And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?
corruption_summary: Importunity is bent into a technique — the name-it-and-claim-it doctrine that treats persistence as leverage over a reluctant God.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief corruption is the prosperity teacher’s reading, in which importunity becomes a spiritual mechanism. Ask with sufficient force, decree with sufficient confidence, refuse to accept the word no, and heaven must yield — as though the Father were the unjust judge of the parable rather than its foil. This inverts the Lord’s argument exactly. He does not say God is like the surly neighbour; He says that if even a surly neighbour yields to knocking, the Father who already knows what you need will not be found less generous. The name-it-and-claim-it scheme also quietly relocates the object of prayer: the friend at midnight asked bread for a traveller, and the widow asked justice, while the modern petitioner is taught to importune for houses, cars, and healings on demand. When the goods do not arrive, the blame falls on the asker’s faith, and a doctrine meant to comfort the persevering saint becomes a whip for the grieving one.

There is a quieter corruption on the other side: the professing believer who does not importune at all, having concluded that since God has decreed the end there is no use in asking. But the same God who ordains the end ordains the crying of His elect day and night as the appointed means of it. Prayer does not change God’s mind; it is the instrument by which He accomplishes what He purposed, and by which He makes His children like Himself in the asking. Hence the parable’s stated aim — that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. Importunity is the posture of Jacob, who would not let go, and of the widow, who would not go away; and the Father who delights to give His Spirit to them that ask has already bound Himself to answer, in His own time and in His own better way, every petition that faith presses at His door.
roots_summary: The word means to press a request without ceasing until it is granted.
roots_lines: Importune — Latin importunus, “troublesome, affording no harbour.”
It names the suit that gives no landing-place, no room to put the asker off.
The friend at midnight receives for his importunity, not his friendship (Luk 11:8).
The widow’s continual coming wore out an unjust judge (Luk 18:5).
Both parables argue upward: how much more the Father of the elect (Luk 18:7).
usage: Importunity is not leverage upon God but the mark of the elect who cry day and night.
Christ gave the parable that men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
The unjust judge is the parable’s foil, never its picture of the Father.

etymology: A compacted phrase, in so much, from Old English in + swa + micel; hence “to such a degree,” “so much so that” — a conjunction of consequence, introducing the effect that followed.
biblical_def: Insomuch is the Authorized Version’s conjunction of consequence: it means to such a degree that, and it always points forward to a result. It must be carefully distinguished from its near neighbour inasmuch, which points backward to a reason. Where the AV says insomuch that, it is measuring an effect: the thing was so great that this followed. So the multitude sees the dumb speak and the lame walk, “Insomuch that the multitude wondered… and they glorified the God of Israel” (Mat 15:31). So the palsied man rises with his bed, “insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God” (Mar 2:12). So the apostolic power in Jerusalem was such that the sick were laid in the streets for Peter’s shadow (Act 5:15). The little word is therefore a measuring-rod laid against the works of God, and the reader who skips it loses the writer’s emphasis. It measures evil as well: the dissembling at Antioch went so far that “Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation” (Gal 2:13) — the hypocrisy was of such a degree that even a good man, the son of consolation who had fetched Saul from Tarsus, was swept along. And the Lord warns of deceivers whose signs shall be such that, were it possible, they should deceive the very elect. Insomuch asks the reader to stop and take the measure of the thing described, whether mercy or madness.
webster_summary: So that; to such a degree that — a conjunction introducing the consequence or effect.
webster_full: INSOMUCH, so that; to such a degree; used to introduce a consequence.
A compacting of the phrase in so much — in so great a measure.
It always looks forward to an effect, never backward to a cause.
Distinguish from inasmuch, which gives a reason: seeing that, because.
The healings were such, insomuch that the multitude wondered (Mat 15:31).
scriptures: Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel.
Mar 2:12
And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion.
Act 5:15
Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them.
Gal 2:13
And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation.
corruption_summary: No modern movement has redefined a conjunction; the loss is that readers now skim the very words by which Scripture measures its own wonders.
corruption_paragraphs: The live danger is not redefinition but blindness. Modern reading habits move fast, and the small connectives of the Authorized Version are the first casualties. A reader who does not know that insomuch introduces a consequence, and that inasmuch introduces a reason, will glide over both and lose the shape of the argument. Worse, he will confuse them, and confusion between a reason and a result is the seed of a great many bad readings — the classic case being Mat 25:40, where inasmuch is regularly heard as though it were insomuch, turning a stated ground of judgment into a supposed effect of good works. Scripture is written tightly; the Spirit gave the joints as well as the bones. To read the Bible for its stirring phrases while skipping its logic is to read it as a devotional scrapbook rather than as the word of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the old Protestant habit of grammatical reading: God has spoken in real sentences, and the sense of a sentence is carried as much by that, therefore, insomuch, wherefore as by its nouns. The Reformers built the recovery of the gospel on exactly such reading — Luther on a Greek preposition, the whole doctrine of imputation resting on how a clause is joined. Every place the AV says insomuch that, it is inviting wonder: look how far this went. The multitude wondered and glorified the God of Israel; a paralytic walked out through the crowd; and, on the darker side, even Barnabas was carried away. Read the joints, and the wonder and the warning both land where the Spirit aimed them.
roots_summary: The word means “to such a degree that” — it introduces a consequence.
roots_lines: Insomuch — a compacting of in so much, in so great a measure.
It is a conjunction of RESULT: the thing was so great that this followed.
Inasmuch is its opposite number, a conjunction of REASON: seeing that, because.
The AV uses it to measure mercy (Mat 15:31; Mar 2:12; Act 5:15).
It also measures evil: the dissembling reached even Barnabas (Gal 2:13).
usage: Insomuch that = so much so that; it names the effect, never the reason.
Do not confuse insomuch with inasmuch: one gives the result, the other the ground.
Where the AV says insomuch, it is asking the reader to take the measure of the thing.

etymology: A literal English rendering of the Latin ablative absolute non obstante, “not standing in the way”; hence “although this stands against it,” “nevertheless” — the obstacle is granted, and then overruled.
biblical_def: Notwithstanding is the Authorized Version’s great word of overruling. It does not deny the obstacle; it grants it and then walks past it. Its native strength appears in Php 1:18, where Paul, bound in prison and preached against by men of envy and strife: “What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.” The bad motives are real and are not excused — and they do not stand in the way of the gospel’s spread nor of the apostle’s joy. That is the whole doctrine of providence compressed into one connective: God’s purpose is not contingent upon the goodness of the instruments. The same word puts joy in its right order when the seventy return elated: “Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luk 10:20). Power over devils is granted — and overruled by election. At the end, deserted at his first answer, Paul writes, “Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me” (2Ti 4:17). All men forsook him; the obstacle is granted; the Lord stood. So also 1Ti 2:15 turns the sentence upon Eve toward hope. Wherever the AV says notwithstanding, a Christian may look for the sovereign hand that lets the difficulty be exactly what it is and accomplishes His will through it anyway.
webster_summary: Nevertheless; however; without hindrance from — the obstacle granted and then overruled.
webster_full: NOTWITHSTANDING, without hindrance or obstruction from; nevertheless; however.
Literally not withstanding — the thing named does not stand in the way.
An English calque of the Latin non obstante, a formula of legal overruling.
It concedes the obstacle honestly, then declares it insufficient.
Paul: notwithstanding, every way Christ is preached, and I therein do rejoice (Php 1:18).
scriptures: Php 1:18
What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion.
Notwithstanding she shall be saved in childbearing, if they continue in faith and charity and holiness with sobriety.
corruption_summary: The word survives; what has been lost is the doctrine it carries — that God overrules real obstacles without pretending they are not there.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern corruption is not of the word but of the comfort it carries, and it comes in two forms. The first is the denial of the obstacle: a cheerful religion that tells the afflicted their trouble is not really trouble, that the envy is not really envy, that the loss is not really loss. Scripture never does this. Paul names the pretence as pretence and the strife as strife, and only then says notwithstanding. Honest naming is the precondition of real comfort. The second form is the denial of the overruling: the practical unbelief that grants the obstacle full weight and stops there, as though the church’s enemies, the preacher’s bad motives, or the saint’s own weakness could halt the purpose of God. Both errors flee the sentence Paul actually wrote, which holds the wound and the victory in a single breath.

The principle to recover is providence in its confessional strength: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and He works even through the crooked instruments of envious men without being the author of their sin. The gospel preached out of contention is still the gospel; the sermon of a man whose heart is wrong still carries a word that is right, and the Spirit still saves by it. That is not indifference to the preacher’s heart — Paul elsewhere warns such men severely — but it is a wall against despair for saints who look at the state of the church and conclude the cause is lost. It never is. All men forsook Paul; notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him. Devils submitted to the seventy; notwithstanding, their names in heaven were the better joy. Learn the word, and learn to say it in the dark.
roots_summary: The word means “this does not stand in the way” — nevertheless.
roots_lines: Notwithstanding — literally not withstanding, not standing against.
An English calque of Latin non obstante, the lawyer’s clause of overruling.
It grants the obstacle honestly, then declares it powerless to stop the end.
Php 1:18 makes it the hinge of providence: Christ is preached either way.
2Ti 4:17: all forsook Paul — notwithstanding, the Lord stood with him.
usage: Notwithstanding never denies the difficulty; it grants it and overrules it.
Christ is preached of envy and of good will — notwithstanding, Christ is preached.
Rejoice not that devils submit; notwithstanding, rejoice that your name is written in heaven.

etymology: A frozen phrase, al be it — “although it be (that)” — from Middle English al (“although”) + the subjunctive be + it; hence a concessive conjunction, granting a point while pressing past it.
biblical_def: Albeit is although it be that, worn smooth into a single word. It is a concessive: it admits something true, then sets it aside for the sake of the main claim. The Authorized Version uses it twice, and both places repay attention. The first is Paul’s masterstroke of pastoral tact in the letter to Philemon. Having offered to pay Onesimus’s debt himself — “If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account” (Phm 1:18) — the apostle adds, “I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides” (Phm 1:19). He declines to press the debt, and in declining, presses it. Philemon owes Paul his very soul, for Paul preached Christ to him; the apostle mentions the thing by refusing to mention it. This is not manipulation but the ordinary courtesy of grace: he will not command what he would rather have willingly. The second use is a thunderclap against false prophets: “have ye not spoken a lying divination, whereas ye say, The LORD saith it; albeit I have not spoken?” (Eze 13:7). Granted that you said it; granted that men believed it; the LORD did not speak. The little concessive there separates the mouth of a man from the mouth of God, and by that separation the whole doctrine of Scripture’s authority stands or falls.
webster_summary: Although it be; notwithstanding that; albeit — a concessive conjunction granting a point in passing.
webster_full: ALBEIT, although it be; notwithstanding; although.
A compacting of the phrase al be it — all (though) it be that.
It grants a point for the moment and then presses on to the main claim.
Paul to Philemon: albeit I do not say how thou owest me thine own self (Phm 1:19).
Ezekiel to the false prophets: ye say, The LORD saith it; albeit I have not spoken (Eze 13:7).
scriptures: Phm 1:19
I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides.
Eze 13:7
Have ye not seen a vain vision, and have ye not spoken a lying divination, whereas ye say, The LORD saith it; albeit I have not spoken?
Phm 1:18
If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account;
Phm 1:21
Having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee, knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say.
corruption_summary: The word is archaic and undisputed; the live danger is the sin Ezekiel met with it — men who say “the LORD saith it” when He has not spoken.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the one Ezekiel exposed with this very word: prophecy in the LORD’s name that the LORD never gave. It is not a museum sin. Modern charismatic movements have industrialised it — the New Apostolic Reformation, the conference platform where a man declares “thus saith the Lord” over a stranger’s marriage or finances, the personal prophecy that fails and is quietly forgotten. Deu 18:22 gives the plain test and it is not softened by sincerity or by good intentions. The dictionary is cessationist because the canon is closed: God has spoken finally in His Son (Heb 1:1–2), and the sufficiency of Scripture leaves no vacancy for new revelation. Every “God told me” that binds another man’s conscience without a chapter and verse is a lying divination, albeit the speaker means well.

The principle to recover on the other side of the word is Paul’s. Notice what the apostle does not do: he does not command Philemon, though he says plainly he might have. He lays out the debt of grace, declines to press it, and then trusts a Christian brother to do more than he says. That is how authority behaves among the redeemed — real, honestly named, and deliberately restrained, appealing rather than compelling, because a grudging obedience is worth nothing to Christ. Elders who have learned this word will find they can carry more weight by leaning on it less. And behind Paul’s put that on mine account stands the greater imputation it images: Christ assuming the debt of runaways, and the Father receiving them as He would receive the Son.
roots_summary: The word means “although it be that” — a concession granted and passed over.
roots_lines: Albeit — Middle English al be it, “although it be (that).”
A concessive: it admits a point and then presses past it.
Twice in the AV — Phm 1:19 and Eze 13:7.
Paul mentions Philemon’s debt by declining to mention it (Phm 1:19).
Ezekiel divides the mouth of man from the mouth of God (Eze 13:7).
usage: Albeit = although it be that: the point is granted and then set aside.
Paul presses Philemon’s debt by the very act of refusing to press it.
They said, The LORD saith it — albeit He had not spoken; that is a lying divination.

etymology: From whither (“to what place,” Old English hwider) + so + ever; hence “to whatever place at all,” an adverb of unrestricted destination — wherever one may go, without exception.
biblical_def: Whither asks to what place; whithersoever answers, to any place at all, without exception. It is the AV’s word of unlimited scope, and Scripture puts it in two great settings. The first is promise. To Joshua on the edge of Jordan the LORD says, “turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest” (Jos 1:7), and again, “be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Jos 1:9). The presence is not bounded by geography. There is no province of the map, and no province of providence, where a man who keeps the law of God walks out from under the covenant presence. The second setting is discipleship, and there the word is put in a man’s mouth as a vow: “Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest” (Mat 8:19). The Lord answers that offer by naming the cost — the Son of man hath not where to lay his head — because whithersoever is easy to say and dear to keep. Ruth spoke the same unbounded loyalty in other words: whither thou goest, I will go (Rut 1:16), and she meant it into a foreign land and a widow’s poverty. James takes the word into a parable of the tongue: great ships are turned about with a very small helm “whithersoever the governor listeth” (Jas 3:4). Small rudders steer whole lives.
webster_summary: To whatever place; to any place at all, without restriction of destination.
webster_full: WHITHERSOEVER, to whatever place; to what place soever.
From whither (to what place) + so + ever, an intensive of scope.
Distinguish whither (to a place) from whence (from a place) and where (at a place).
The LORD is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Jos 1:9).
A ship is turned whithersoever the governor listeth (Jas 3:4).
scriptures: Jos 1:7

Only be thou strong and very courageous, that thou mayest observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded thee: turn not from it to the right hand or to the left, that thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
Mat 8:19
And a certain scribe came, and said unto him, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest.
Jas 3:4
Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.
corruption_summary: A promise of unbounded presence is turned into a promise of unbounded success, and a vow of unbounded loyalty is reduced to a slogan.
corruption_paragraphs: Jos 1:7–9 is among the most abused passages in modern religious speech. Lifted off a wall calendar or a locker-room poster, thou mayest prosper whithersoever thou goest becomes a guarantee of worldly success attached to no condition whatever. The text conditions it plainly: prosperity is joined to observing to do according to all the law which Moses commanded, turning neither to the right hand nor to the left, and meditating in the book day and night. Strip the condition and you have not encouragement but a lie, and one that will fail every man who leans on it in a hard providence. The promise given to Joshua concerned the conquest of a land under a covenant; what carries over to the Christian is not a guarantee of outcomes but the surer thing — the presence: the LORD thy God is with thee, the same presence Christ pledged to the end of the world.

The other corruption is cheap discipleship. I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest is sung with feeling by people who have never counted what the word covers, and the Lord’s reply to the scribe is the permanent rebuke: foxes have holes and birds have nests, and the Son of man hath not where to lay his head. Whithersoever includes the places you would not choose. Ruth’s version of the vow carried her out of her nation and her gods into a stranger’s poverty and gleaning behind the reapers, and the LORD honoured it into the line of David and of Christ. Covenant loyalty is not measured by the warmth of the promise but by the ground it is kept on. Say the word if you will, but know that Christ takes it literally, and that He kept His own version of it to a cross.
roots_summary: The word means “to whatever place at all” — destination without restriction.
roots_lines: Whithersoever — whither (to what place) + so + ever.
Old English hwider, motion toward; not where (rest) nor whence (from).
It names unlimited scope of destination, no province excepted.
Promise: the LORD is with thee whithersoever thou goest (Jos 1:9).
Vow: Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest (Mat 8:19).
usage: Whithersoever means to any place at all — the covenant presence has no border.
Joshua’s prosperity is joined to the law observed, not detached as a slogan.
The scribe said whithersoever; Christ answered with the price of the word.

etymology: A compacting of the phrase in as much (as); hence “in the same measure that,” “seeing that,” “because” — a conjunction of reason or ground, not of result.
biblical_def: Inasmuch as means seeing that, in the very measure that, because. It gives a ground, not an effect — the opposite office from insomuch, which gives a result. The AV uses it to state the reason a thing is so: Christ is counted worthy of more glory than Moses, “inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house” (Heb 3:3); Paul magnifies his office, “inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles” (Rom 11:13). Its most famous appearance is in the judgment of the sheep and the goats: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me” (Mat 25:40), and the dread converse, “Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me” (Mat 25:45). Two things must be seen there. First, the word identifies rather than rewards: the King is not saying that mercy purchased the kingdom, but that mercy shown to His brethren was mercy shown to Him, and so is the evidence by which the sheep are known. The inheritance was “prepared for you from the foundation of the world” — before any cup of water was given. Second, the objects are named: my brethren, and the least of them. Christ so identifies with His own that what is done to the meanest believer is reckoned as done to Him.
webster_summary: Seeing that; since; in the same measure that — a conjunction giving the reason or ground.
webster_full: INASMUCH, in like degree; seeing that; since; considering that.
A compacting of the phrase in as much as — in the same measure that.
It always gives a REASON or ground; it never states a consequence.
Distinguish from insomuch, which introduces the effect that followed.
Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren (Mat 25:40).
scriptures: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Then shall he answer them, saying, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.
Heb 3:3
For this man was counted worthy of more glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house.
For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office:
corruption_summary: Mat 25:40 is the great hostage text of the social gospel — severed from “my brethren,” from faith in Christ, and from the sovereign election that precedes the works.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant corruption is the social-gospel reading, which takes inasmuch as a doctrine of salvation by service. On that reading Christ is present in every needy person as such, the “least of these” becomes a class defined by material want or by the fashionable political category of the “marginalized,” and the judgment turns on relief work rather than on union with Christ. Three things refute it from the text itself. First, Christ says my brethren, and He has already told us who those are: whosoever shall do the will of My Father, the same is My brother (Mat 12:50) — the persecuted disciples sent out with nothing, whose reception or rejection is the reception or rejection of the One who sent them (Mat 10:40–42). Second, the kingdom is prepared for you from the foundation of the world; the sheep are sheep before ever a hungry man is fed, and the works are the evidence of an election that long preceded them. Third, the sheep are astonished — Lord, when saw we thee? — which no man is who has been totting up merits. Justification is by faith alone; the faith that justifies is never alone.

The opposite corruption must be named as well, because Reformed readers are prone to it: having rightly refused salvation by works, some empty the passage of any claim at all, as though mercy to the poor saint were optional trimming. It is not. The goats are condemned for nothing they did — only for what they did not do, and their damnation is as eternal as the sheep’s life. A profession that leaves the brother naked and unvisited is a dead profession (Jas 2:15–17), and the King will say so on that day. The right reading holds both: the works do not purchase the kingdom, and their absence proves it was never inherited. And the sweetness in the word remains — Christ so identifies with the least of His people that the cup of cold water given to an obscure believer is received by the Lord of glory as given to Himself, and He will name it aloud before the assembled nations.
roots_summary: The word means “seeing that, in the measure that” — it gives a ground, not a result.
roots_lines: Inasmuch — a compacting of in as much as.
A conjunction of REASON: seeing that, since, because.
Its near neighbour insomuch is a conjunction of RESULT — do not confuse them.
Mat 25:40 states the ground of the King’s verdict, not the price of the kingdom.
The objects are named: the least of these MY BRETHREN.
usage: Inasmuch gives a reason; insomuch gives a result — the difference decides Mat 25:40.
The kingdom was prepared from the foundation of the world; the works only identify the heirs.
Christ reckons the cup of water given to the least believer as given to Himself.

etymology: From the Latin communicare, “to share, to make common” (communis, “common”), through the Old French communer; hence to converse, to confer, to hold intercourse — to have a matter in common between two.
biblical_def: To commune is to converse, to confer, to hold speech with another so that a thing becomes common between you. The Authorized Version uses it at three heights. Highest is the LORD communing with man from the appointed place: “there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony” (Exo 25:22). Mark where the speech happens — over the blood-sprinkled lid that covers the broken law. God does not commune with sinners in the open air; He communes from above the mercy seat, and the antitype is Christ, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation. All fellowship with God is mediated fellowship, or it is none. Second is the soul’s communing with itself: “Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” (Psa 4:4). This is the lost art of self-examination — the man taking his own heart aside for a hearing, in the dark, where there is no audience to impress. Asaph does it in his distress: “I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search” (Psa 77:6). Third is ordinary conference between men, which may be holy or wicked: the disciples on the Emmaus road “communed together and reasoned” and Jesus Himself drew near (Luk 24:15), while the scribes, filled with madness, “communed one with another what they might do to Jesus” (Luk 6:11).
webster_summary: To converse; to confer; to talk together familiarly — to hold intercourse of thought.
webster_full: COMMUNE, to converse; to talk together familiarly; to impart sentiments mutually.
From Latin communis, “common” — to make a matter common between two.
Used of God speaking with man, of a man with his own heart, and of men together.
The LORD communes from above the mercy seat (Exo 25:22).
Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still (Psa 4:4).
scriptures: And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel.
Psa 4:4
Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah.
Psa 77:6
I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.
And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.
corruption_summary: Communing with God is detached from the mercy seat and made a bare mysticism, while communing with one’s own heart is replaced by an age that cannot be still.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is unmediated communion. Modern religion is full of talk about encountering the divine directly — contemplative techniques, centring exercises, the inner voice trusted as God’s own — with no altar, no blood, and no Mediator in sight. Exo 25:22 forecloses it. God appointed one place and one only from which He would commune, and that place was above the mercy seat, over the sprinkled blood, between the cherubim who had once barred Eden with a flaming sword. The lesson stands for the New Covenant: there is one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, and the veil was rent from the top down by His death, not by our ascent. Any fellowship with God claimed apart from the propitiation is a fellowship with something, but it is not with the LORD.

The second corruption is the death of self-examination. Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still assumes both solitude and silence, and our age has abolished them. The bed is now the place of the glowing screen; the last waking thought is somebody else’s content, and the first is the same. Where there is no stillness there is no communing, and where there is no communing with one’s own heart there is no repentance, for a man cannot confess what he has never sat down and looked at. The Puritans made this a discipline and called it keeping short accounts. Nor is the remedy morbid introspection, which is only self-communing without the mercy seat; the examination that heals always ends where it began, over the blood, at the throne of grace. Search the heart, and then take what you find there to the place where God has promised to speak.
roots_summary: The word means to converse, to confer — to make a matter common between two.
roots_lines: Commune — Latin communis, “common,” through Old French communer.
To hold speech together so that the matter becomes common to both.
God’s communing has an appointed place: from above the mercy seat (Exo 25:22).
A man may commune with his own heart — self-examination in stillness (Psa 4:4).
Men commune together for good (Luk 24:15) or for murder (Luk 6:11).
usage: God communes from above the mercy seat — all fellowship with Him is mediated.
Commune with your own heart upon your bed: the lost discipline of self-examination.
The Emmaus disciples communed and reasoned, and Jesus Himself drew near.

etymology: From the Old French enquerre, from the Latin inquirere, “to seek into” (in-, “into,” + quaerere, “to seek”); the AV’s spelling of inquire — to ask, to seek an answer, and especially to seek an oracle.
biblical_def: To enquire is to seek into a matter and ask for an answer; in Scripture it is chiefly a technical word for seeking a word from God. The whole question of true and false religion turns on the object of the verb. Israel was to enquire of the LORD — through the priest, the ephod, the Urim, the prophet, and above all the written word. David’s one desire is “to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple” (Psa 27:4); the enquiring is set in the appointed house, by the appointed means. Against that stands Saul on his last night: “Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her” (1Sa 28:7). Heaven had gone silent — by dreams, by Urim, by prophets — and rather than repent, Saul went to Endor. The Chronicler pronounces the verdict without pity: Saul died “for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it; And enquired not of the LORD” (1Ch 10:13–14). Ahaziah did the same toward Ekron and was met with the angel’s withering question, “Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron?” (2Ki 1:3). Here is the regulative principle in seed: God appoints not only that He shall be sought, but how and where. To seek Him by means He has not commanded is to seek another god under His name.
webster_summary: To ask; to seek into a matter; and especially to seek an oracle or counsel from God.
webster_full: ENQUIRE (also inquire), to ask a question; to seek information by asking.
From Latin inquirere, “to seek into” (in- + quaerere, to seek).
In Scripture chiefly technical: to seek a word or oracle from the LORD.
David desired to dwell in the house of the LORD and to enquire in his temple (Psa 27:4).
Saul enquired of a familiar spirit and enquired not of the LORD, and died (1Ch 10:13–14).
scriptures: Psa 27:4
One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple.

Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor.

So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;

But the angel of the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say unto them, Is it not because there is not a God in Israel, that ye go to enquire of Baalzebub the god of Ekron?
corruption_summary: Endor is not extinct: the age enquires of horoscopes, mediums, and inner impressions, and the church enquires by means God never appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: The old sin of Endor is thriving under new names. Astrology columns, tarot decks, mediums selling contact with the dead, spirit boards sold as games, and the whole apparatus of neo-pagan divination — these are exactly what Saul went to, and Deu 18:10–12 calls them an abomination to the LORD. Isa 8:19 puts the absurdity in one line: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead? The bereaved are the most preyed upon, and the medium’s trade is to sell a counterfeit of the resurrection to people who need the real one. Whether a given practitioner is a fraud or is genuinely trafficking with unclean spirits, the verdict is the same: it is enquiring of a familiar spirit, and it is the sin for which the first king of Israel died.

The subtler corruption is inside the church, and it is a matter of means. God appoints not only that He be sought but how: in His word read and preached, in the ordinances, in prayer, in the counsel of godly elders. Against this the age sets a religion of impressions — opening the Bible at random for a sign, laying out fleeces, waiting on an inner voice, seeking a personal prophecy from a platform, choosing a spouse or a calling by a feeling reported as the voice of God. All of it enquires by means the LORD has not commanded, and the regulative principle answers it: what Scripture has not appointed is not permitted. David’s desire is the pattern — to dwell in the house of the LORD and to enquire in His temple, which is to say, to seek God where God has promised to be found. Enquire there, and He is found; enquire elsewhere, and something answers.
roots_summary: The word means to seek into a matter — and in Scripture, to seek an oracle from God.
roots_lines: Enquire — Latin inquirere, in- (into) + quaerere (to seek).
The AV’s spelling of inquire; the same word, the older orthography.
Technical sense: to seek a word from the LORD by His appointed means.
Saul enquired of a familiar spirit and not of the LORD (1Ch 10:13–14).
David enquired in the temple — the right God sought in the right place (Psa 27:4).
usage: The whole of religion hangs on the object of the verb: enquire of whom?
Saul enquired at Endor because he would not repent; it cost him his life and his kingdom.
God appoints not only that He be sought but by what means — that is the regulative principle.

etymology: From the Old English intensive prefix be- + stirian, “to stir, to move”; hence to rouse oneself into vigorous action, to put oneself briskly in motion — almost always reflexive, to bestir thyself.
biblical_def: To bestir oneself is to rouse up and move — to shake off delay and act with vigour. The word appears once in the Authorized Version, and it stands at one of Scripture’s clearest joinings of divine sovereignty to human means. David, twice attacked by the Philistines in the valley of Rephaim, will not fight without asking; and the LORD gives him a sign and an order together: “And let it be, when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines” (2Sa 5:24). Every part of that verse deserves weight. The sound in the treetops is God’s doing, not David’s; the going forth of the LORD before the army is the whole cause of the victory; and yet David must bestir himself, and the battle must be fought by men with swords in their hands. The Chronicler’s parallel says it plainly: “then thou shalt go out to battle: for God is gone forth before thee” (1Ch 14:15). Note the word for — God’s prior going is the reason David moves, not the excuse for standing still. This is the exact logic of Php 2:12–13: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do. Sovereignty does not cancel means; it commands and guarantees them.
webster_summary: To put into brisk or vigorous action; to rouse oneself and move — used reflexively.
webster_full: BESTIR, to put into brisk or vigorous action; to move with life and vigour.
Usually with the reflexive pronoun: bestir thyself, bestir themselves.
From the intensive be- + Old English stirian, “to stir, to move.”
A KJV hapax: thou shalt bestir thyself at the sound in the mulberry trees (2Sa 5:24).
The parallel reads, then thou shalt go out to battle (1Ch 14:15).
scriptures: And let it be, when thou hearest the sound of a going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt bestir thyself: for then shall the LORD go out before thee, to smite the host of the Philistines.

And it shall be, when thou shalt hear a sound of going in the tops of the mulberry trees, that then thou shalt go out to battle: for God is gone forth before thee to smite the host of the Philistines.
Php 2:12
Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.
Php 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
corruption_summary: The one-word command of 2Sa 5:24 is lost to two opposite errors — the fatalism that will not move, and the activism that moves before the sound.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error is a counterfeit of Reformed doctrine and is found among people who ought to know better: since God has decreed the end, why bestir myself? Why evangelise, why labour in prayer, why fight sin, when the outcome is fixed? The answer is written into the verse. The LORD goes out before David — and David goes out too, and the Philistines are smitten by Israelite swords. God ordains the means as surely as He ordains the end, and the man who pleads sovereignty as a reason for sloth has not believed the doctrine, only borrowed its vocabulary to excuse himself. The confession that God ordains whatsoever comes to pass is the very ground of diligence, because it guarantees the labour is not in vain in the Lord.

The opposite error is activism — the church that never waits for the sound in the mulberry trees. David’s first victory in that valley came by enquiring; his second came by enquiring again, and the LORD gave a different order the second time. A man who had merely repeated the previous method would have marched at the wrong hour. Much modern ministry runs on borrowed strategy and busy machinery, forgetting that the treetop sound is the only thing that makes the going out anything but a slaughter. The pattern to recover is neither passivity nor presumption but the ordered obedience of a servant: enquire, listen, and then bestir yourself with everything you have, because the LORD has gone out before you. Watch and pray; then rise and fight.
roots_summary: The word means to rouse oneself into vigorous action — to stir and move.
roots_lines: Bestir — intensive be- + Old English stirian, “to stir.”
Reflexive by habit: a man bestirs himself; no one bestirs another.
A KJV hapax, at the sound in the mulberry trees (2Sa 5:24).
The sign is God’s; the going forth is God’s; the bestirring is David’s.
Its doctrine is Php 2:12–13 — work, FOR it is God which worketh in you.
usage: Bestir thyself: the sovereign LORD goes before, and the soldier still draws his sword.
The sound in the mulberry trees is God’s signal, not David’s strategy.
Sovereignty is the ground of diligence, never the excuse for sloth.
